claims.text: A machine-learning model integrating vibrational spectra and atomic-scale disorder descriptors can identify low-phonon-thermal-conductivity high-entropy alloys more accurately than conventional models.
The intended materials are single-phase, homogeneous high-entropy alloys dominated by random substitutional disorder.
The proposed model uses alloy composition, computed vibrational-mode spectra, and disorder-induced scattering indicators to predict phonon thermal conductivity.
Atomic-scale disorder enhances anharmonic and strain-induced phonon scattering.
Local variations in atomic occupancy and vibrational behavior enhance phonon scattering.
Enhanced phonon scattering caused by local atomic and vibrational variations reduces thermal conductivity.
High-dimensional vibrational and disorder descriptors establish a stronger quantitative composition–thermal-transport relationship than conventional averaged-property methods.
The proposed model will improve agreement with experimental measurements by approximately 15–30% relative to traditional methods.
Conventional models based on average mass or force-constant fluctuations, or limited empirical correlations, tend to overestimate phonon thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys.
The anticipated predictive improvement applies primarily to single-phase, homogeneous high-entropy alloys dominated by substitutional disorder.
The anticipated improvement may not apply to alloys with significant phase segregation, extreme atomic-size mismatch, or microstructures dominated by grain-boundary scattering.
The magnitude of predictive improvement may vary among compositional subspaces because of variation in alloy complexity.
A decisive comparison can be made by measuring matched single-phase alloy samples under identical conditions and comparing errors from conventional and machine-learning models.
Failure of the machine-learning model to reduce mean prediction error by at least 15% relative to conventional methods would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The boundary excludes significantly multiphase alloys from the model's applicability, but the falsification rule says detection of significant multiphase behavior in tested alloys falsifies the hypothesis. Such detection would instead show that the benchmark violated the stated inclusion criteria.

The rule treats a 15% reduction in mean error as equivalent to a 15–30% improvement in prediction accuracy, although error reduction and accuracy improvement are not necessarily equivalent without a precise metric and definition.
